opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a great question, and honestly, for a lot of people the answer is: you shouldn't, at least not at first. Start with an off-the-shelf model, see how far prompting and maybe some fine-tuning get you. Llama 2 is a fantastic gift to the community, and for many use cases it's going to be good enough.

But there are a few reasons people come to us wanting to train their own models, and they tend to fall into a handful of buckets.

The first is data. A lot of enterprises are sitting on enormous amounts of proprietary data, whether that's years of internal documents, code, customer interactions, or domain-specific material in finance, biology, or law. That data looks nothing like the web crawl these general-purpose models were trained on. You can fine-tune on it, sure, but if you have tens or hundreds of billions of tokens of your own data, there's a real argument for baking that knowledge in from the start, or at least doing substantial continued pretraining. The model you get really understands your world rather than having a thin veneer of it.

The second is control. When you take someone else's model, you inherit every decision they made: what data went in, how it was filtered, what tokenizer they used, what languages it covers, what safety tuning was applied. You often don't actually know what's in that training set. For companies in regulated industries, or ones that worry about licensing and provenance, being able to say "we know exactly what this model saw" is enormously valuable. And then there's the licensing itself. Llama 2's license has conditions, and some organizations want something they fully own.

Third is cost and efficiency at inference time. A general-purpose 70-billion-parameter model is trying to be good at everything. If you only need it to be excellent at one thing, you can often train a much smaller model that matches or beats it on your task and is dramatically cheaper to serve. When you're running millions of queries a day, inference cost dominates, and a custom smaller model pays for itself pretty quickly.

And the last thing I'd say is that training has gotten a lot cheaper than people think. There's this perception that pretraining is something only a handful of labs with hundreds of millions of dollars can do. That's just not true anymore. With the right infrastructure and good recipes, training a really capable model from scratch is within reach for a lot of organizations, on the order of hundreds of thousands of dollars rather than tens of millions. Once that's the case, the calculus changes. It's not "should I spend an impossible amount of money," it's "is this a reasonable investment given what I get back."

So I don't see it as open models versus custom models. It's a spectrum. Prompt an existing model, fine-tune it, do continued pretraining, or train from scratch, and the right answer depends on your data, your constraints, and your scale. What we want is for people to have the freedom to pick the point on that spectrum that's right for them, rather than being stuck with whatever someone else decided to build.

r001.rationale: The response describes proprietary data that differs from general models’ training data, but does not say that no existing model is available for that domain.

r002.rationale: It says a custom smaller model can match or beat a general-purpose model on a specific task, identifying better task performance as a reason to train custom.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so this is the question I get asked more than any other, and I think it's a great question. Llama 2 is a wonderful model. I'm thrilled it exists. But I'd push back a little on the framing that there's one model that's good for everyone, because that's just not how we've seen things play out when we actually work with customers.

The first reason is data. If you're a company that has a lot of proprietary data, a lot of domain-specific data, that data is your differentiator. Llama 2 has never seen it. It was trained on the public internet, and the public internet doesn't contain your legal documents, your customer support logs, your codebase, your medical records, whatever it is. You can try to get at that with retrieval or with prompting, and sometimes that works, but there's a limit to how far you can get by bolting things onto a model versus actually having the knowledge baked in. So a lot of folks start by fine-tuning, and some of them end up pretraining from scratch because the domain is far enough away from general web text that it's worth it.

The second reason is control. When you use someone else's model, you're inheriting all of their choices: what data went in, what got filtered out, what the tokenizer looks like, what the context length is, what the license permits. Llama 2's license, for example, has restrictions that matter to some businesses and not others. If you train your own model, you know exactly what's in it, you own the weights, you can run it wherever you want, and nobody can take it away from you or change the terms on you six months from now. For a lot of enterprises, that's not a nice-to-have, that's a requirement.

The third reason, and this is the one people underestimate, is cost and efficiency. A general-purpose model has to be good at everything, so it has to be big. If you only need to be good at one thing, you can often get there with a much smaller model that's trained specifically for that task, and a smaller model is cheaper to serve, faster, and easier to deploy. We've seen customers replace calls to a very large general model with a model that's an order of magnitude smaller, trained on their own data, and get equal or better quality on the thing they actually care about.

And then I'd say the last reason is just that the economics have changed. A couple of years ago, training a model from scratch was something only a handful of labs could do. That's not true anymore. The cost has come down dramatically, the tooling is much better, and the recipes are much better understood. So the question isn't really "should I use Llama 2 or train my own." It's "what's the right tool for this problem." Sometimes the answer is the open model. Sometimes it's fine-tuning the open model. And increasingly, for people with real data and real stakes, the answer is to build their own. I think all of those are going to coexist, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you only one of them matters.

r001.rationale: The response says public models lack companies’ proprietary, domain-specific data and that sufficiently different domains may justify training from scratch.

r002.rationale: It says customers can replace a large general model with a custom model and get better quality on the task they care about.

astra-6.text:
Llama 2 is a great starting point, and for a lot of people, a publicly available model may be all they need. But that model wasn’t trained specifically for your task, on your data, or with your constraints in mind.

Say you’re using a model for one narrow task. You might not need all the capabilities of a large general-purpose model. You might want a much smaller model that does that one thing well, because it’s cheaper to run and responds faster. Or you might have specialized data and terminology that the model doesn’t handle particularly well out of the box.

And training a custom model doesn’t necessarily mean starting from scratch. It could mean fine-tuning an existing model. The question is really: what’s the simplest, most cost-effective way to get the behavior you need? Public models give you a fantastic starting point, but they don’t eliminate the value of adapting a model to your particular problem.

r001.rationale: The response says existing models may not handle specialized data or terminology well, but does not say that no model exists for the domain.

r002.rationale: It says a public model may not handle specialized data particularly well out of the box, giving a reason to adapt a model for better task-specific performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is whether you need to train a model at all. If an existing model does what you need, great—use it. Training a model shouldn’t be the goal; solving your problem should be the goal.

But something like Llama 2 is a general-purpose model. It hasn’t necessarily been optimized for your particular task, your data, or the constraints of your application. You might need it to understand specialized terminology, produce a very specific kind of output, or do one narrow thing reliably. And if you can get that behavior into a smaller model, you may be able to serve it much more cheaply and with lower latency.

There’s also a spectrum here. Training a custom model doesn’t necessarily mean starting from scratch. You can take an existing model and fine-tune it. The question is: how much customization do you need to get the quality and cost you want? Publicly available models give you a fantastic starting point, but that doesn’t mean they’re the best endpoint for every application.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose models may not be optimized for a specific task or terminology, but does not identify the absence of an existing model for a particular domain as a reason to train one.

r002.rationale: It explains that a public model may not provide the quality or reliability an application needs, and that customization can improve task-specific behavior.
